lesson.title: Bonjour & Merci
lesson.subtitle: Greetings, thanks, and ça va — the politeness set in dialogue

hook.title: Words You Must Never Convert
hook.content: Bonjour is not 'good journey' and merci is not 'merchant's fee' in this context — some words you simply take as whole items. Bonjour (good day), merci (thanks — mercy's coin), oui (yes), s'il vous plaît (if it pleases you). These are the handshake of the language: small, fixed, and everywhere.

footnotes.title: merci and mercy
footnotes.content: Latin mercēs 'wages, reward' gave French merci and English mercy. Thanking someone is acknowledging what you owe — the coin is the same in both languages.

pattern.title: ça va — the Conversation That Answers Itself
pattern.content: Ça va ? — 'it goes?' — is the everyday how-are-you. The answer is the same two words: ça va. Greeting culture also has the bise (cheek kisses, count varies by region) and the tu/vous decision — vous for strangers and formality, tu for friends. When in doubt: vous. Nobody was ever fired for vous.

footnotes.title: The T–V line
footnotes.content: tu/vous is the same politeness ladder as German du/Sie and English's lost thou/ye. French kept the ladder standing; English knocked its own down.

pattern.trap_note: Don't over-convert: bonjour is one word, not 'bon jour' to be rebuilt. Idioms are items, not formulas.

exercises.prompt: Match each politeness formula with its use:
exercises.target_answer: Bonjour, Merci, S'il vous plaît, Oui, Ça va ?
exercises.explanation: Five fixed items — taken whole, used whole.

exercises.prompt: A stranger at the bakery — which pronoun do you reach for?
exercises.explanation: Strangers, elders, officials: vous. Friends, children, dogs: tu. When in doubt, vous.

exercises.idea: you're ordering politely: a coffee, please (formal)
cues: the politeness tag: s'il vous plaît
exercises.explanation: The politeness escalator starts here — topic 26 will upgrade it to je voudrais.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the French way?
options: How are you? — I am fine, thanks
exercises.meaning: The odd English is the lesson: aller (to go) carries the greeting.
exercises.explanation: ça va is literally 'it goes'. The question and the answer are the same sentence, tilted.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.affirmation: You spelled beaucoup as one word — the amplifier stays welded.

summary.outcome: Deploy the handshake set, choose vous under pressure, and answer ça va with itself.

use_example.german: Bonjour ! Ça va ? — Ça va, merci.
use_example.english: Hello! How's it going? — Fine, thanks.

summary.takeaway: Idioms are items, not formulas — and vous is the pronoun you can't be fired for.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "A coffee, please" in French:
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Un café, s'il vous plaît" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of Bonjour & Merci.

bonjour.etymology_derivation: bon 'good' + jour 'day' (Latin diurnum) — English's 'good day' is the same thought, German's Guten Tag too.

merci.etymology_derivation: Latin mercēs 'wages, reward' — thank-you and mercy are the same coin: what you owe.

oui.etymology_derivation: worn down from Vulgar Latin hoc illud 'yes indeed!' — a yes so emphatic it wore itself into one syllable.

sil_vous_plait.etymology_derivation: 'if it pleases you' — politeness as a small conditional; compare 'if you please', which English still owns.

vous.etymology_derivation: Latin vōs 'you all' promoted to politeness — the same T–V ladder as German Sie and English's lost 'ye'.

tu.etymology_derivation: Latin tū — the very word the King James Bible still whispers as thou. Point your lips; the vowel is not English's.
